title: Hello [Open] World: Unbody Is Now OSS (Alpha)
author: amir
blurb: Unbody announces the release of its open-source Alpha, introducing a modular, AI-native backend designed to be the "Supabase of the AI era." This release invites developers to build on an infrastructure that mirrors human cognition through perception, memory, reasoning, and action.

summary.summary: This is the first modular backend for the AI-native era built together in the open.
It is a data knowledge driven, AI-native backend designed to replace traditional stacks.
The system is architected for modularity, autonomous agent support, and plugin extensibility.
We are building the Supabase of the AI era and inviting you to help shape it.
The project is available at github.com/unbody-io/unbody.
Launching commercially last year as a backend-as-a-service revealed truths about AI-native development.
One truth became clear: we weren’t going to build an excellent product without involving the wider developer community.
We are releasing Unbody as open source to build a better product and gain developer adoption.
We believe open source is critical for building trust, transparency, and user control in intelligent systems.
This alpha release focuses on architectural flexibility and modularity rather than feature completeness.
The modular design supports both traditional plugins and autonomous AI agents.
The Contextual Data Engine transforms raw data into structured, queryable, and interconnected knowledge.
The architecture is designed for integration with tools like Unstructured.io and LlamaIndex.
Our open-source version already outclasses our cloud service in terms of architectural openness.
Our cloud offering includes production-grade features but comes with trade-offs like locked-in storage.
The open-source version gives greater flexibility to choose storage solutions and AI models.
The content API remains unchanged despite significant refactors in data ingestion and processing.
Our roadmap envisions the eventual replacement of our cloud version with this open-source powerhouse.
We are sharing Unbody OSS Alpha to open a discussion with the wider community.
The AI tooling ecosystem is scattered, requiring developers to stitch together complex stacks.
We ask what if there were a Supabase, but for the AI era.
Supabase simplified building web apps by handling databases, auth, and storage in a unified stack.
Unbody aims to bring that spirit to AI-native software that reasons, adapts, and acts.
Supabase is great, but it wasn't built for a world where your backend needs to think.
Stacks built around storing static data in tables are insufficient for AI-native products.
The way we interact with software has fundamentally changed.
We no longer just click buttons; we talk to software and expect it to reason.
AI-native software is active and context-aware, requiring a backend that manages dynamic knowledge.
AI-native software needs enriched, connected knowledge rather than just rows in tables.
Software needs a dynamic, evolving graph of meaning to mimic human intelligence.
Data ingestion, vectorization, and summarization are essential infrastructure, not extras.
A backend must ingest and process images, video, and audio to understand like a human.
It is a Supabase-style stack for building AI-native products from the ground up.
Without Unbody, even building a simple Q&A bot requires complex setup.
You usually need to spin up a vector database like Weaviate or Pinecone.
You need to create a pipeline for chunking and ingesting content.
You have to stitch all this into your backend and maintain it.
Unbody is built for opinionated flexibility, allowing you to bring your own vector store or AI provider.
This image shows the Unbody modular stack architecture.
Please see the README on our GitHub repo for in-depth information.
If software is becoming more like humans, the backend needs to work like a brain.
Unbody is built on four functional layers that mirror how intelligent systems operate.
The Perception layer handles how the system sees and understands the world.
The Memory layer handles what the system knows and remembers.
The Reasoning layer handles how the system thinks, decides, and plans.
The Action layer handles how the system interacts via APIs and MCP.
This is where raw data becomes structured, enriched knowledge.
Data Ingestion connects and pulls content from third-party platforms or local files.
Processing automatically parses and structures raw multi-modal data.
Enhancement employs agents to transform raw data into a more semantic knowledge base.
Vectorization generates semantic vector representations using various AI models.
This is where your enriched knowledge lives, ready to be retrieved.
Vector Storage places embeddings in databases like Weaviate, Pinecone, or Qdrant.
File Storage persists raw and processed files locally or in the cloud.
Media Serving provides access to media through Unbody’s CDN.
The Metadata Store keeps track of content structure and relationships.
This is where intelligence happens, including generation and decision-making.
Text Generation includes built-in support for hosted or self-hosted models like GPT-4.
JSON Generation produces structured responses and machine-readable payloads.
Image Generation is a roadmap item for cloud-only visual generation.
The Function Registry defines callable functions via schema-based definitions.
Execution & Routing dynamically executes functions with intent parsing and argument validation.
This is where your backend connects to the outside world via APIs and SDKs.
The Content API lets you query your knowledge base via GraphQL.
The Push API allows you to push structured data directly into Unbody.
The Admin API configures schemas, projects, pipelines, and permissions.
The MCP connects Unbody to external systems and workflows.
SDKs are available in TypeScript, iOS, and Android.
Chat endpoints include memory and long-term context.
Integration with observability monitoring systems is supported.
We are in feedback mode and want to know what works and what breaks.
We invited you to give Unbody Alpha a try and provide feedback.

title: The End of the Container Era: Apps Are a Historical Glitch
author: amir
blurb: Software containers are a 'historical glitch' that force humans to act as routers between disconnected apps. It's time to move beyond the App Era toward an architecture based on intent and threads, not rigid boxes.

summary.summary: We accept the friction and fatigue of modern work because we lack a name for it.
This feeling is actually a symptom of a specific architectural failure.
We incorrectly assume that Apps and Websites are the natural laws of software.
Software containers are a 'historical glitch' that emerged from macro-level constraints, not human thinking.
Software had to be packaged into standalone units or 'containers' due to distribution limitations.
Vendors needed to ship one static interface to millions of users due to server constraints.
Logistical hurdles made software something designed first and used second, forcing us into rigid boxes.
The resulting system is built on three anti-human pillars.
In the digital world, you must travel to the tool, unlike the physical world where tools come to you.
You are forced to 'go to' specific locations like Gmail or Salesforce to perform actions.
These boxes are walled gardens of logic that result in visiting disconnected rooms over and over.
This physical separation creates a deeper cognitive fracture.
Previous research confirms we are trapped in the 'Page Era,' a centralized model of predefined UI.
The 'Page' forces a model where the server decides what the container looks like top-down.
Humans explore chunk-by-chunk via threads, but software is built on Pages and Apps.
The OS forces you to translate your intent into its rigid language because it only understands containers.
Visualizing the disconnect shows the server shipping Pages while the mind follows Threads.
Tabs are the ultimate symptom of the OS failing to understand the thread of your work.
We pay a price because the logic is siloed and the abstraction is wrong.
You act as the 'human router' manually copying context between boxes that don't talk to each other.
The result is a quiet insanity of 32 tabs and infinite micro-searches.
You pay this tax with your attention, time, and nervous system.
The energy is shifting in the builder community as the dam finally breaks.
Innovators like Naval Ravikant and AGI Inc are proving the future is about pure intent, not menus.
Teams like Zo and Wabi AI are exploring browser-native clouds and personal software fitting the user.
We are circling the truth that the 'use' of software is the bottleneck, not the build.
A social post reflects on the bottleneck of software usage.
We need to rethink the architecture so the 'app' doesn't need to exist, creating a layer deeper than agents.
This is Part 1 of a series that will introduce the 'Faceless Data Layer' next.
We are cooking up something in stealth that tackles exactly this.

Before discussing management, we must first define generative data.
Generative data is any output produced on the fly by a model rather than fetched from a static database.
To keep the discussion grounded, we will use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as the main example.
To clarify the concept, it helps to contrast generative data with the CRUD model we already understand.
An image compares generative data against CRUD data.
RAG is a pattern combining a user's question with relevant data sources to generate a response.
An image illustrates the RAG flow of retrieve, generate, and respond.
The first step is retrieving relevant content such as documents or database records from your data.
The second step is generating an answer using that retrieved content as context.
This setup grounds the generation in real, retrievable context instead of relying solely on training data.
This flow serves as the working example for the concepts discussed in this post.
In CRUD flows, data is a complete fact that arrives after a standard request lifecycle.
In generative flows, the response is an interpretation built in real time, often streamed and varying.
The distinction between fact and interpretation leads to three fundamental differences in thinking about state.
A typical CRUD request is atomic, consisting of one request and one response.
An image depicts the atomic one-shot nature of CRUD requests and responses.
In RAG and most generative workflows, the process involves at least two stages.
An image shows a minimal multi-stage pipeline consisting of retrieval and generation.
A realistic setup often includes more steps than just the minimal case.
An image details a realistic multi-stage generative pipeline with additional steps.
Since each stage can fail or stream independently, a single loading flag breaks the state model.
Unlike CRUD payloads typically arriving at once, generative flows stream data over time.
Streaming can be sequential, non-monotonic, or involve refinement depending on the model type.
Without thinking in terms of partial state and streaming updates, the UI will be unresponsive or erratic.
An image compares traditional parcel delivery to streaming token-by-token output.
Here is a simplified example of how generative output is typically handled in practice.
You do not receive the data all at once but must build it as it arrives.
In CRUD flows, the data is a precise, repeatable, and complete fact.
An image contrasts CRUD returning facts against generative systems returning interpretations.
Generative responses are interpretations shaped by input, context, and probability rather than facts.
Even with identical input, the generated output can vary in tone, wording, or structure.
While the CRUD response is the truth, the generative response is merely a version of the truth.
This distinction fundamentally changes output predictability and how it should be treated in the UI.
Understanding that generative data is multi-stage and interpretative necessitates a change in state management.
Generative endpoints often return a readable stream of text tokens rather than a complete result.
Instead of setting a final result, you must append tokens as they arrive.
You also need to support canceling the stream immediately to save costs and handle user changes.
An image visualizes the need for append and cancel support during streaming.
Failing to support cancellation leads to burning tokens unnecessarily.
Without append logic, you cannot reflect progress in the UI.
Context is the real state you need to manage.
The UI reacts to a pipeline where the composition of stages like retrieval and generation forms the context.
You should treat the context as a first-class application state object rather than a one-off response.
A structured context in a RAG system includes elements like retrieved records and conversation history.
An image shows a sample context structure for a RAG system.
A common mistake is discarding the intermediate states and records that made the output possible.
Discarding context essentially means throwing away the trace of your reasoning.
This context object represents the actual state of your generative UI.
The frontend component should be bound to this context, persisting what the model saw.
When users regenerate or edit, this context serves as the single source of truth.
The context becomes a contract stating that the output is the best interpretation given those inputs.
The system implies that given this specific context, the result is its best interpretation.
Preserving context makes it easier to explain why the model generated specific outputs.
Understanding generation as a pipeline leads to a shift in how you model state in your UI.
A simple loading flag is insufficient in gen flows because multiple steps have distinct behaviors.
Your app needs to treat each stage of the pipeline as its own state machine.
Union types guarantee that you are never in conflicting states like being both loading and done.
State machines allow you to give precise feedback to the user about specific stages.
This approach allows you to retry only part of the flow, such as just the generation step.
Using a switch on state makes managing UI logic much easier.
In generative flows, retries are considered a feature rather than just error handling.
Sometimes you need a retry because the model failed or you simply want a second version.
Since every stage is separate, retries should also be stage-aware.
An image illustrates a stage-aware retry flow in generative pipelines.
Managing UI state involves tracking context and building a UI that reflects the actual pipeline stages.
These principles apply to any UI built on top of generative outputs, including RAG and LLM tools.
The author is considering a follow-up post focused on implementation-level patterns if there is interest.
The author invites feedback from those building generative features and interested in developer ergonomics.

title: AI in 2023: Paradoxical Advancement
author: amir
blurb: Despite incredible technological leaps in 2023, a significant gap remains between AI advancement and its practical application in business. This essay explores why industries like law and healthcare are underutilizing AI and how low-code platforms can bridge this divide.

summary.summary: This text focuses on bridging the increasing gap between AI as tech and its applications.
As 2023 draws to a close, a critical observation emerges regarding the stark contrast between technological leaps and their real-world applications in the business sector.
AI's potential to transform passive data into actionable knowledge remains largely untapped, which is not due to AI's inability but its limited practical application.
This section outlines examples of Untapped AI Potential in Industries.
We dive into specific industry scenarios to highlight how AI's transformative potential remains largely untapped.
In the Legal Sector, AI can automate and expedite case research, yet this application is rarely seen in practice.
In the Healthcare Industry, AI has the potential to revolutionize patient diagnosis, yet its adoption is sporadic and largely confined to experimental segments.
The Publishing Industry continues to rely heavily on traditional methods, with AI-driven innovations being more of an exception than the norm.
While AI could be a powerful tool, its practical application in addressing these industry-specific challenges is still in its nascent stages.
The complexity of AI technology is a significant factor contributing to its limited application in business.
Tools that are technologically sophisticated aren't always user-friendly, presenting a barrier to their widespread adoption in everyday business operations.
Input from a broader range of professionals is crucial for transforming AI from a complex, niche technology into a user-friendly tool.
Unbody was created as a low-code privacy-friendly platform to democratize AI technology and make tools accessible to a wider audience.
We are ready to explore ways we can help law firms, websites, and publishing effectively use AI.
The key to unlocking AI's full potential in business lies in bridging the gap between its technological capabilities and practical applications.

title: From Query to Context: Building Agentic RAG with Unbody's JSON Endpoint
author: amir
blurb: Discover how to upgrade from naive RAG to robust Agentic RAG by parsing natural language queries into structured parameters using Unbody's generative JSON endpoint. This guide walks through extracting context, applying precise filters, and generating accurate responses for complex user constraints.

summary.summary: The author discusses the limitations of naive RAG systems compared to robust approaches presented at AI Thinkers Abu Dhabi.
A complex user query example is provided: an Italian dish for two, no sausage, ready in under 30 minutes.
Agentic RAG helps by parsing the query into structured parameters for precise retrieval instead of relying on naive systems.
The article proposes showing how to implement this system with Unbody step by step.
Step one requires an Unbody project set up with data, such as a collection of recipes, already ingested.
Step two involves obtaining the API key and Project ID directly from the Unbody dashboard.
Users who haven't set up a project yet are directed to the Unbody docs for a quick start guide.
With setup complete, developers can start calling Unbody’s APIs to search, filter, and generate.
Knowing the data schema is essential to efficiently extract parameters from a user's query, such as in a recipe collection.
The schema dictates what information is available and helps decide which parts of the user query should be parsed.
A specific user query example is cited requesting an Italian dish with no sausage in under 30 minutes.
From the query, the system knows to extract the concept, ingredients to exclude, and a time constraint.
RAG consists of Retrieval and Generation, where retrieval is crucial for gathering context for the model.
The first retrieval approach involves taking the user’s entire query as a single text string.
The next step in the naive approach feeds the top documents into a text-generation prompt.
Naive systems fail with multiple constraints because they do not actually understand the user’s intention.
The first step in an Agentic approach is to parse the user’s query into structured parameters.
The second step is to apply filters to the knowledge base based on the parsed parameters.
The third step involves generating the final response using only the documents that are truly relevant.
The syntax implementation utilizes Unbody’s chain syntax methods for execution.
Translating to a proper RAG query requires extracting three specific pieces of information.
The first piece is the main keywords or concepts from the query for semantic search.
The second piece involves identifying any specific filters to pass to the where function.
The third piece is extracting the prompt or task description for the generate function.
Unbody’s generative JSON endpoint and the Zod library are used to validate and define the model output.
Unbody’s generative JSON syntax accepts arguments for message role definitions and a Zod schema.
The Zod schema defines the shape of the generative JSON, starting with the extraction of a concepts field.
The schema expects an array of strings or null if no concepts are extracted.
The describe method is used to add notes explaining that a field represents main search terms.
The schema captures ingredients the user wants to include following the same method as concepts.
A description clarifies that the field is for ingredients the user explicitly wants in the recipe.
The schema is expanded to include all fields expected from the query, such as cuisine types.
One of the expanded fields is includeCuisineTypes for identifying preferred cuisine types.
Another field is totalTimeMinutesMax used to set a maximum time constraint.
The full Zod schema is presented with descriptions provided for every field.
A queryParser function is created to integrate the entire logic now that the schema is complete.
The complete querySchema is passed to the generative endpoint within the function.
A system message is set to instruct the model to analyze the user's query.
The returned payload provides a well-structured object containing all extracted parameters after validation.
This snippet creates a structured JSON object from the user's input for use in precise queries.
Creating the final RAG pipeline begins after parsing the query into detailed parameters.
Search logic uses extracted concepts if available, otherwise it falls back to the full query.
Prioritizing specific keywords ensures the semantic search remains as focused as possible.
The complex part of the process involves turning extracted filters into proper where clauses.
If the query includes ingredients, a filter is added to match the includeIngredients array.
A conditional check handles cases where includeIngredients is not provided in the query.
The code conditionally spreads the filter if ingredients exist or adds an empty array if not.
Filters are added conditionally for ingredients to exclude, such as when a user says no sausage.
Excluded ingredients are mapped into a NotEqual filter and added only if they exist.
The section discusses combining all filters using the And operator.
All the individual filters are combined into a single query object.
The final combined filter checks each parameter and adds a condition only if that parameter exists.
The final answer is generated using the generate fromMany method.
The generation step produces a final coherent answer after retrieval and filtering.
The system message instructs the model to generate a response considering the retrieved results.
The complete RAG pipeline is assembled in the final section.
A full API handler example is shown, typically for use in a Next.js project.
The parseQuery function processes the free-form query and returns a structured object with parameters.
Semantic search focuses on the extracted concepts found in the parsed object.
The where function applies each filter conditionally using the And operator logic.
The autocut method limits the result set to keep it manageable.
The generate fromMany method produces a coherent answer integrating the retrieved documents.
A full demo of the Agentic RAG system is available to watch on YouTube.
Developers interested in the code can find the complete source on GitHub.
A specific GitHub link is provided for the recipes example project.
Unbody’s Agentic RAG approach captures intention and filters precisely by breaking down complex queries.
The author asks if the reader is ready to build smarter AI-native applications.
Readers are encouraged to experiment with the sample code to tailor their own Agentic RAG pipeline.
The Unbody documentation is recommended for further insights and advanced use cases.
Creators are invited to share projects and join the conversation on community forums.
Developers passionate about AI-native development are encouraged to join the open-source community.
The post concludes by encouraging builders to push the boundaries of what applications can do.

title: What the F**k is an AI-native app?
author: amir
blurb: AI-first is becoming the new mobile-first, but what defines an AI-native application? This post explores the shift towards adaptive, human-centric software and details the technical architecture required to build it.

summary.summary: This post dives into the characteristics of AI-native apps as AI-first becomes the new mobile-first mindset.
The shift in user mentality establishes a dialogue with software, necessitating a corresponding shift in design where AI functionalities will become standard.
An AI-native app is defined as a more human software that understands us and can adopt to the human user.
Software should adapt and tailor to our individual needs and contexts, such as the different roles we embody at work versus at home.
A chatbot must understand your specific company and personal responsibilities to effectively search documents or summarize reports.
We need software to access and understand the data footprints we produce daily to provide a prioritized user experience.
Traditionally, managing data for apps involves using CMS to curate and restructure content, which requires considerable manual effort.
An illustration compares traditional versus AI-native data management approaches for personalization.
Conventional methods require re-curating existing content like PDFs and Docs to fit structured data requirements and manually applying tags.
AI-native applications bypass traditional steps by utilizing language models to adapt data in its original format and location.
The process requires the capability to aggregate and process documents and data from all different locations and platforms.
The second crucial aspect is context, which involves linking isolated data points similar to the principle behind Hypertext.
An image visualizes context awareness achieved through semantically connected data sources.
Context involves making connections between different islands of information, such as technical documentation and community slack discussions.
Semantic search enables a deeper understanding and linking of content to provide contextually connected responses.
Users now expect to communicate with apps and websites through conversation, rather than just seeking information by clicking options.
An image depicts the user behavior shift from simple information seeking to conversational interaction with software.
The growing preference for natural human language interaction requires apps to develop capabilities for deeper semantic analysis.
To support interactive approaches, we need features like generative search, image captioning, and content classification.
A diagram illustrates the technical breakdown of various AI-native app components.
The essential technology for AI-first apps breaks down into data aggregation, data processing, and functions.
Data Aggregation focuses on getting data from different places and making sure it all syncs up nicely.
Data Processing involves turning raw data into enhanced AI-ready data through cleaning, chunking, and vectorizing.
The functions division borrows from RAG but goes beyond it to avoid getting too technical.
Data Retrieval acts as a supercharged search engine inside your app to help you find exactly what you need quickly.
Data Augmentation makes existing data better by adding new details or tweaking it to understand different scenarios.
Data Generation creates new bits of content right on the spot based on what users are asking for, borrowing from RAG principles.
This section offers a peek at what it looks like to assemble a system that can handle all the discussed components.
An image displays the complexity involved in assembling a full AI-native system from scratch.
Building this system requires familiarity with Python and assembling components like document parsers, embeddings, and LLM APIs.
Beyond AI elements, real-world apps require functionalities like CDNs and video hosting, making development challenging.
Unbody is developing an AI-as-a-service platform that automates the entire AI development pipeline to solve these challenges.
A visual explains how Unbody simplifies the process of AI-native app development.
Unbody automates the aggregation and processing of data from any source and format, from Google Drive to local video files.
The platform streamlines AI model management by handling complexities of upgrades and deployments for models like OpenAI's GPTs.
Unbody enables delivery to the developer via an API or SDK, making integration as simple as writing a single line of code.
A video demonstrates a short semantic search implementation in JavaScript.
Developers can just connect data, select an AI stack, and start building with one line of code.
The author shares examples of open-source AI-native products built using Unbody.io.
